1.title: The Aromatic Pink Mutation of the Savagnin Family
1.html:
Gewurztraminer is the aromatic, pink-skinned variant of Savagnin Blanc. Its origin is debated, but it is generally believed to be a selection from a musky Traminer. Alsace documented this variety as early as 1551 (in botanist Bock's Kreuterbuch).

This variety also has a non-aromatic variant — known in Alsace as "Heiligensteiner Klevener", today's Klevener de Heiligenstein, a supplementary geographical denomination within AOC Alsace limited to the villages around Heiligenstein (covered in depth in Level 2).
2.title: Fruit Characteristics and Viticulture
2.html:
• Bunch: small, conical, rather loose
  • Berry: small oval, pink to light red, thick-skinned, with intense flavour and a faint muscat note
  • Ripening: early to mid (2e époque hâtive), moderate yields (46–56 hl/ha)
3.title: Wine Style and Food Pairing
3.html:
Style: noble, grand, full-structured, with a highly recognisable intense aroma — delicate, strong and elegant. Although mostly dry in good vintages, Alsace winemakers customarily keep a little residual sugar so that aroma and palate harmonise better; it has good ageing potential and keeps its floral character for a long time.

Young, fresh style: smoked salmon, poached turbot, veal cutlet with tomato coulis
Young style: aperitif, or with a VT version
Full style: exotic cuisine, curry; ideal with strong cheeses such as Munster and Roquefort
Aged style / VT: fresh or pan-fried foie gras, hot pastry pies, Alsatian tarts
SGN: perfect to end a meal
4.question: Why does Alsace Gewurztraminer often keep a little residual sugar even when made in a dry style?
4.options.0: Because natural fermentation cannot convert all the sugar
4.options.1: Because winemakers find that a little residual sugar makes aroma and palate more harmonious and balanced
4.options.2: Because regulations require a minimum residual sugar
4.options.3: To lower costs by shortening fermentation
4.explanation: Gewurztraminer is usually dry in good vintages, but Alsace winemakers deliberately keep a little residual sugar — not because of a technical limitation, but because a moderate amount lets Gewurztraminer's intense aroma and palate show in a more harmonious balance, an important aesthetic choice in the Alsace winemaking tradition.
